content: Index fossils, also referred to as guide fossils or zone fossils, are specific types of fossils that are utilized to define and identify particular geologic periods or faunal stages. The principle behind their use is that, although sedimentary layers may appear different due to the environmental conditions under which they were deposited, they can still contain the remains of the same species of fossil. If the species in question had a relatively short lifespan in geological terms—lasting only a few hundred thousand years—then the sediments containing these fossils must have been deposited within that specific, narrow time frame. The shorter the lifespan of the species, the more precisely geologists can correlate different sedimentary layers. For this reason, fossils of species that evolved rapidly are especially valuable for this purpose. The most effective index fossils are those that are abundant, easily identifiable at the species level, and widely distributed geographically. Without these characteristics, the chances of finding and recognizing the same fossil in different sedimentary layers are significantly reduced. Ammonites are an excellent example of index fossils, as they meet these criteria well and are among the most widely recognized and utilized fossils for this purpose. Other important groups that serve as index fossils include corals, graptolites, brachiopods, trilobites, and echinoids (commonly known as sea urchins). Conodonts, which are microscopic, tooth-like fossils, can also be identified by experts using light microscopy and are valuable for providing precise age determinations of sedimentary layers. Additionally, fossilized teeth of mammals have been employed in certain cases for similar purposes. Geologists rely on both large fossils, known as macrofossils, and microscopic fossils, referred to as microfossils, in the process of biostratigraphy. Macrofossils have the advantage of being easily visible in the field, but they are less common. On the other hand, microfossils are more frequently used, particularly by industries such as oil exploration, where accurate dating of rock layers is critical for resource identification and extraction.
